what: The ceilings an ordnance marker is held to, written once for both languages.
why: Every one of these is a clamp the server enforces and the client used to restate - and every
one of the four had drifted, all in the same direction: the client allowed 120 / 48 / 48 / 240
where the service clamps 72 / 24 / 24 / 120. A restored snapshot therefore drew a 48-dice salvo
on screen that the server halved to 24 the moment anything touched it, and nothing said so.
The direction of the drift is what makes it worse than a mismatch: the client being the wider
of the two means the screen shows a number the engine will never honour, so the table plans
against it. A client narrower than the server would be the other failure - refusing a value the
engine would have accepted - which is the shape that once made a stationary ship unturnable.
These are shape bounds, not rules numbers: they bound what a marker may carry rather than
stating anything about missiles, so they sit outside the content-policy guards deliberately,
for the same reason the ship-form bounds do. What was missing was the other half of that
argument - the pair could drift silently, and did, four times over.
ordnanceBounds.test.ts reads them back through normalizeMatchSnapshot, the front door the app
actually calls, and OrdnanceBoundsParityTests drives CreateOrdnanceMarker and reads the snapshot
back. Both restore paths clamp to the same numbers (InMemoryMatchService.Restore.cs), so a
change on either side reddens one of the two suites.
whyEachFloorIsZero: A marker that entered nothing has entered nothing - there is no floor of one salvo, one die or one inch anywhere in this app, and inventing one would be this app writing a number the player owns.
